utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you, Madam Registrar. Could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. This is case number IT-03-67-PT, the Prosecutor versus Vojislav Seselj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, madam. Mr. Seselj, can you follow the proceedings in your own language?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Daniel Saxon for the Prosecution, Your Honour, with my colleague, Mr. Ulrich Mussemeyer, assisted by our case manager, Ms. Ana Katalinic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And stand-by counsel?

utterances.speaker: MR. VAN DER SPOEL
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour, Tjarda van der Spoel, stand-by counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you and good morning to you as well. The reason for this Status Conference is the requirement of Rule 65 bis to hold a Status Conference more or less every 120 days to organise exchanges between the parties with a view to ensuring expeditious preparation for trial and to review the status of the case and to allow the accused the opportunity to raise issues in relation to the status of his case and in relation to his mental and physical condition and also matters relating to his state of detention. The last Status Conference was held on the 26th of September, 2005 and therefore we are holding this Status Conference within the 120-day limit. The reason why we are holding it so early in the morning is because I had a request from the accused himself, which I found justified by all means, and I had the cooperation of the parties in another case to delay the commencement of the hearing of the sitting in the other case later until this is finished. So I will just report first on some of the events that have occurred between the last Status Conference and this one. And I will start first by informing you that at the latest, Tuesday or Wednesday of next week, we will hand down the decision on electronic disclosure of documents of the accused which is long overdue, but we had plenty to discuss and finally we have come to a decision. It's receiving the final polish and it should be out, I'll sign it on Tuesday after last meeting with the other two judges or latest on Wednesday. There is, then, the matter of a request by the accused for material cited in the Prosecution's pre-trial brief. This goes back to December 2004. It was submission number 67 from the accused, and the Prosecution, when filing its pre-trial brief on the 14th of December stated that it would eventually provide the witness and exhibit list. Subsequently, the -- we had the accused submission number 67, as I said, and the Prosecution responded to it on the 18th of January. This is an ongoing matter involving not only the pre-trial brief and the witness list and the exhibit list but also other matters related that I will touch upon as we go along. One thing that I will be mentioning later on is that in view of developments the pre-trial brief that you had filed earlier on in the proceedings will have to be refiled with an update reflecting the amendments to the indictment. And touching on the indictment, I must say that on the 22nd of October of 2004, the Prosecution requested leave to amend the indictment, which had already been confirmed, originally been confirmed on the 14th of February of 2003. My Trial Chamber on the 27th of May, 2005 granted the Prosecution's request in principle, designating the Prosecution's proposed amended indictment as the operative indictment while it ordered minor clarifications. Subsequently on the 3rd of June of last year, the Prosecution filed a corrigendum to the amended indictment clarifying the part referred to by the Trial Chamber, and the Trial Chamber on the 8th of July granted the corrigendum in part and ordered the Prosecution to file a modified amended indictment accordingly. The Prosecution filed the modified amended indictment on the 12th of June 2000 -- July 2005, and on the 8th of September of last year, the accused filed his submission 101, to which I will be referring again later on, and preliminary motion number 102 pursuant to Rule 72 of the -- our Rules of Procedure and Evidence challenging the modified or amended indictment. Inter alia, he submitted once more a challenge to the legality of the ICTY and alleged defects in the form of the modified amended indictment. The Prosecution filed its response to submission number 101 and also to preliminary motion 102 and -- on the 16th of September 2005, and basically it was pointed out to the Trial Chamber, pre-trial Chamber that the length of the accused's motion was far beyond the limitation set in the practice direction and Prosecution consequently requested the Trial Chamber to refuse to receive the motion and directed accused to prepare a new motion in the proper format before the 7th of October, 2005. On the 23rd of September of last year, I issued a decision in which I refused to accept the accused's preliminary motion and gave him the chance to file his objections, if any, by the 7th of October in the format prescribed by the practice directive. On the 10th of October, 2005, the accused filed his submission number 111 in which he requested certification to appeal my decision of the 23rd of September, 2005 and then extension of the deadline for raising objections to the modified amended indictment until such time as he has received a translation into the Serbian language of judgements from -- certain judgements from the ICTR, the Rwanda Tribunal. The Trial Chamber denied the accused's requests, and on 17th of November, 2005, he filed his submission number 119, in which he requested certification to appeal the Trial Chamber's decision on submissions 110 and 111 on the grounds that the denial of certification to appeal constituted a denial of his right to submit objections to the modified amended indictment. A decision is pending on this motion. On Tuesday, this coming Tuesday, the other two Judges and myself are going to meet specifically to finalise our decision on this matter. So in all probability, Wednesday, I will sign the decision on disclosure, and towards the end of the week, I will sign the decision on your request for certification. But Mr. Seselj is not the only one who is seeking certification. There is also the Prosecution that is seeking certification in relation to our decision on the sixth motion for protective measures for witnesses which we gave, I think, on the 13th of December, 2005 before we went into recess. This will be considered in due course, as I said, but we are giving priority to the request for certification on the part of the accused, so I cannot exactly state when we will be able to dispose of yours but it should come up immediately after. Then there are two other motions that have been forthcoming from the accused. One is in relation to a request that he has made for the payment by the Registry of 2.339.400 US dollars for expenses incurred by his expert team associated with the preparation of his defence in 2003 and 2005, between 2003 and 2005, and the ultimate motion for the revocation of our long-standing decision to appoint a stand-by counsel in his case. These two motions are also on the agenda I have for the Tuesday meeting with the other two Judges. Basically they have already been considered to some extent by the three of us separately and we have exchanged views on our position, and on Tuesday we should be able to finalise. Whether we should be able to hand down a decision by the end of next week depends on whether Registrar would have filed his comments on the first of these two motions, because we are -- we will be requiring some kind of feedback from the Registrar to see what the position of the Registrar is in relation to this matter. So these are basically the events that have taken place as regards to motion. If you would like to make any comments on any of these motions now, Mr. Seselj, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, I'd like to say something with respect to the motion that has to do with the decision of the pre-trial Chamber that in this case, in these proceedings, the function of stand-by counsel be introduced as it's called. Now, although that decision and ruling was made almost three years ago, it still does not have any legal foundation in the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, let alone the Statute of the international Tribunal. That decision is outside the legal system of this international Tribunal and from that, I deduce that the decision was so distorted in the legal sense that the Judges of this Tribunal did not even make the effort to ground it in law later on subsequently and it exists only in this particular case. In the international military court in Nuremberg, the accused had the right completely freely to decide whether they were going to defend themselves or whether they were to appoint a counsel, and they could have appointed counsel without any criteria set. It would suffice that he was a member of the bar on the list of the bar of any state. Now what is being done here, the arbitrariness of the Secretariat in this case on the basis of a decision and ruling of the pre-trial Chamber dating to 2003, is truly a legal absurdity which must be done away with as soon as possible, at least in the proceedings against me. Perhaps somebody else will find it fairly suitable. Now, with respect to the payment of expenses and costs, the Secretariat is consistently avoiding making a decisive decision. According to the Statute of the international Tribunal, I have the right to receive sums of money. That is what the Statute says. I have received no resources to date, and my expenses run up to 2.300-something thousand dollars. They are objective expenses incurred by concrete work, and I have proof of the concrete work done. The large number of motions, submissions by me, reports and so on and so forth. So none of these points and items have been fabricated. They are well grounded on concrete work expended. Now, the Registry asked me to state what property I owned. I provided them with exact information. As to members of my family, closer family or distant family don't wish to cooperate with the Registry, and it's up to them. My family members are not going to put in their property to finance my defence. The registry would be right to insist upon that if it had a single shred of evidence and proof that I, from the date in which one of these criminal acts allegedly was committed, had -- handed over part of my property to my family members and then you could deduce that I intentionally wanted to leave myself indigent, without the resources to pay for my own defence; however, I never did that. I always regularly stated the property that I had, and in addition to what I have, I demand that the international Tribunal finance my defence. Furthermore, the international Tribunal must bear in mind how the cases were conducted in all the other proceedings, what the expenses for defence were and to see how complicated this case is because there are certain trials which are linked to just one locality and a very limited space of time and then the Defence case costs $4 or 5 million nonetheless, whereas in my case the crimes, alleged crimes have been spread out throughout the whole of the territory of the former Yugoslavia. It is very difficult and complicated to prepare my defence, especially as the Prosecution wishes to ascribe to me the criminal acts of Vuk Draskovic and then sends me documents by mistake and then says -- sends the prison guards to seize the binders that it has provided me with because they disclosed for more than they wished to disclose, and such scandalous acts have been happening within the framework of this case. So you can't keep a secret how much defence expenses ran up to in other cases, whereas the Prosecution says that this is a secret. What secret? It's how the United Nations monies are being spent. It's not a question of protected witnesses. The Prosecution is endeavouring to side-step that obligation it has. And another important question that I wish to raise is this: I am still not able to cooperate normally with my legal advisers and members of the expert team to prepare my defence. I have consistently been putting forward the names of people who are well qualified to be my legal advisers and who proved themselves to be my legal advisers in preparing a large number of court motions, reports and so on and so forth and submissions, whereas the Registry is asking that my legal advisers fulfil the conditions prescribed for lawyers, attorneys. My legal advisers will never be attorneys, will never be Defence counsel in this case, and as Defence counsels I don't need them. I need them the way they stand, how they are, graduated legal men to carry out the work that I wish them to carry out for me, and as long as I'm satisfied with their work, I don't wish to change them, nor do I wish to take somebody else that the Registry of the international Tribunal would impose upon me in its biased nature, and this has been proved many other times in other cases and in my own case. Furthermore, the Registry is asking me that my legal advisers know English or French. Now, to be quite frank, I don't have any confidence in a Serb who knows English and French very well, those languages, because experience has told me that I can't have trust and confidence in people like that. They don't have any need of knowing the French and English languages. The important thing is that they know the Serbian language well, that they can understand what I'm saying and carry out the requests I have made for my proper defence. Another condition was set that my legal advisers were not in a relevant criminal proceedings. I come from a country that has been under communist regime. There is no honest and honourable man who is a prominent intellectual, lawyer or any other profession who lived under the communist regime without having been held criminally responsible at least once in his life for some crime or misdemeanours. Anybody who hasn't been had before the courts was not a moral and decent person during the communist regime. They didn't have the guts to stand up to that regime, so if they have not been proclaimed guilty in some criminal proceedings, I cannot accept them. I only have people who are dissidents and who suffered under the communist regime and by the same token were convicted of some crimes by that regime. Next it says that my legal advisers must be people who did not upset the public's belief and trust in the international Tribunal, go against its image. Now my legal advisers can only be persons who together with me do, in fact, question and challenge the standing of this international Tribunal as an illegal Tribunal because by the end of these proceedings, at the end much this court trial, one of my defence pivotal points will be that I'm challenging its legality. I'm not going to give that up, and nobody can force me to give up that position I'm going to take. So my legal advisers never published confidential material either. They signed agreement with me on disclosure, governing disclosure, binding themselves not to disclose a single confidential piece of material or document which I receive, which I have in my possession and receive from the OTP or the Registry, that this will not come out in public, and that is sufficient. They are fully conscious of the measures governing protected witnesses and the protection of certain confidential documents, and what more can be asked of them to do. However, the Registry would like to force me to take on people that the Secretariat and Registry can influence and therefore upset my defence. These pre-trial proceedings have been going on for three years now, and during those three years, there have been attempts on the part of the Registry to make my defence impossible. And finally I insist upon going to trial as soon as possible. If you don't give me legal advisers, right, you're not going to give them to me, I'm going to go ahead alone. If you don't provide me with all the documents in the Serbian language, right, I'm going to go ahead and I'm trial ready without them. But I would like to remind you of the Nuremberg military tribunal which categorically guaranteed the right of the accused to receive all court material in his own language, every single piece of material, and you're trying to side-step that obligation. Every document must be written down on paper. You don't provide it on paper. You provide if to me in this electronic -- that's up to you. It's up to you. A reasonable time limit for the beginning of trial must be set.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, you have exactly one more minute to finish.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll be finished right away, Mr. Agius. The point is that every reasonable deadline for the start of trial is long over. Your Trial Chamber has evaded stating anything about this. The Prosecution says this is not true. But even had I been on provisional release, this time period would have been too long leading up to the start of trial, let alone having to wait for it in detention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, Mr. Seselj. These matters or those of them that have relevance will be subject matter of our various decisions. Any particular submissions on your side?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. We'll deal with disclosure now. Disclosure under Rule 66(A)(i), following the modified amended indictment, can the Prosecution confirm that any new supporting material has now been disclosed?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: We can confirm that, Your Honour, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can you confirm this, Mr. Seselj, only in relation to disclosure under 66(A)(i), supporting materials, in other words. Answer yes or no, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But I have to remind you that part of this material has been seized from me subsequently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Yes. I'm aware of that. Rule 66(A)(ii) material disclosure. Basically I will restrict this only to the sixth motion for protective measures for witnesses which was filed by the Prosecution on the 5th of October and a decision was reached on the 13th of December. I wish to confirm that this decision is the subject of a request by the Prosecution for certification to appeal. Otherwise I don't think that there is anything else to do about this except to have a confirmation from the Prosecution that otherwise, saving the -- these decisions, you have completed disclosure under Rule 66(A)(ii). Are you in a position to confirm that?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: No, I am not, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Yes. And what is the situation, then?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: We are awaiting the Trial Chamber's decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Of course. I realise that. I said I'm only going to put in this safe compartment the decision on the sixth motion obviously. But apart from that, you have disclosed what you needed to disclose.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Pending that motion, yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, all right. Rule 68 material, is there anything else? I know that this is usually an ongoing process, but is there anything under Rule 68 material that you have dug up which you haven't disclosed as yet?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, pending the Trial Chamber's decision on the form of disclosure, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So that I think the position you understand what has been stated by the Prosecution. Do you wish to add anything, Mr. Seselj? Very shortly, very briefly. Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. There is a big problem concerning the disclosure under Rule 68 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, as regards exculpatory material. The Prosecution is trying to evade this obligation by providing me with inadequate material. I have already drawn the Trial Chamber's attention to this. The rule states that all exculpatory evidence must have something to do with the case against me, if not with the case then at least with me personally. However, the Prosecution is delivering to me, for example, minutes of exhumations of bodies near Prijedor. Prijedor is not even mentioned in the indictment, not a single place in Bosanska Krajina is mentioned -- in Bosnian Krajina is mentioned in my indictment, so what should I do with this material? What use is it to me? The Court should not allow the Prosecution to evade its obligation to disclose Rule 68 material in this way. The Prosecution needs to invest as much energy and time in finding exculpatory material as it does in the finding of incriminating material, and this has been stated before this Tribunal in other cases. The Trial Chamber should prevent the Prosecution from evading or ignoring its Rule 68 obligation and to act according to the Rules of Procedure and Evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Seselj. If there are specific instances where you believe that the Prosecution had in its possession Rule 68 material which it did not disclose to you, then please bring that to the attention of the Trial Chamber and we'll deal with it after having given the Prosecution the chance to deal with the matter too. Rule 65 ter material. Now, here the position is obvious. You had filed a pre-trial brief last December. Due to the newly -- new amended modified indictment, I think we need an updated pre-trial brief. How much time do you require?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Or I suppose that you had thought about this and that you had started working on it; I would presume so at least.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And it is the Prosecution's intention to file its updated pre-trial brief by the end of next week, which would be close of business, 3rd of February, 2006.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. And that will be translated into your language and then you will have an opportunity to come back to us with your response. Are there any other issues that you would like to raise, Mr. Seselj, and then I will ask you as well, before I come to the question of the conditions of your state of detention and your health.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I've said what I had to say today. I only insist that the start of trial be scheduled as soon as possible and that the Trial Chamber decide whether a reasonable time limit has expired or not for the start of trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I thank you, Mr. Seselj. I can assure you that the Tribunal is very anxious to start your case because, as you said, you have been in detention for quite sometime now and that the fact that there has not been a joinder with the other cases that were planned earlier on should provide you an indication that your case will not take long before starting. Otherwise it would have taken longer. So let's come to the conditions of the accused. First of all, I wish to inform you that come March, end of February, March, or at some other point in time during spring in particular, I intend to commission another analysis of the air in your room for purposes of establishing the existence of allergens now that we know what you are allergic to. The indications in the expert's report that we have, that we received sometime back, is that in spring particularly early spring, there might be a change which should be of interest not only to you but also to us. The other thing I wish to mention you -- to mention and ask you about, and if you want me can go into private session about this, that in reading the report I got impression that while you are receiving medication for asthma, you are not receiving medication for your allergies. I don't know if I have read the report well or not, but you are in a better position to know what kind of medication you are receiving. This is something that I noticed in the report and that I wanted to ask you about. If you need my intervention, and that of the other two Judges in this regard, let's start with this first and then we continue with the rest. Yes, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, I think there is no need to go into private session. Mr. Agius, I have already told you that my condition of health should not be a secret to anyone and my health is not so bad that I should be constantly complaining about it. I receive medication for my allergy to pollen in the appropriate season. However, I have never received any medication for allergy to yeasts and moulds because it has only recently been discovered that I am allergic to these, probably because of the conditions in the detention unit. However, there is no medication that is capable of removing all the symptoms of asthma. That's the problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. But what I want to know from you is that -- whether, following the report by the expert, you have been receiving the right treatment and the attention you require, or whether you have any specific complaints that you would like to make to me, the reason being that I will attend to those complaints straight away.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm still receiving the same medication I received before. Nothing has changed. As for the conditions, they have worsened for all accused in the meantime. They have all been to the -- moved to the building in which I am, and now, of course, there is no use asking to be moved back to a building that no longer exists, but if I were to get a cell with more light, more sunshine, my health condition might improve. But I won't insist on that. There are far more serious problems here, so in the past few months as you may have noticed I am no longer stressing this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but are there any points related to your health or to the state of detention that you would like to raise before we adjourn?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The most serious problem I'm facing is the problem of photocopying. I have about a thousand handwritten pages of text, densely written text. You know how densely I write, Mr. Agius. I must photocopy this in order to give copies to the members of my expert team so that they can make use of this material in their further projects. I'm not able to do this because the detention unit authorities are not permitting me to photocopy. That is the minimum requirement I have. They have provided me with an additional cell but I haven't used it in a year. I don't need an additional cell. I need photocopying facilities. They keep giving me something I don't need while consistently evading providing me with things I do need.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: With regard to photocopying, you know that we -- we are fully aware of your request. We know that you requested the commanding officer of the unit and that subsequently you are aware that the Registry filed a confidential and ex parte submission stating that it was not the responsibility of UNDU to provide clerical support to the accused. We made sure that you were aware of the Registrar's position and objections, reflecting, of course, the position of the commanding officer after you rightly so filed your submission number 114 requesting that the Registrar's position be made --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is a problem in the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So -- can you receive interpretation now?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Some words are being used which I don't understand "tajnistvo," "tajnik," and so on. These expressions do not exist in the Serbian language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. You have to live with that, Mr. Seselj. I understand that the difference between those words and the corresponding word in the Serbian language sometimes is of just one letter. Anyway, there was submission number 114 on your part requesting to have access to the Registrar's submission because the Registrar's submission had been filed confidential and ex parte. We granted you this, but we also stated that it is not a duty or the responsibility of the UN Detention Unit to make photocopies for you, since you had chosen a -- to defend yourself. If you want to make copies, you obviously need to make your own arrangements. That's the position taken by us. I do not have on record, at least I don't recall having it on record, that you asked for certification to appeal from this judgement, unless I am wrong. Is there anything else you would like to raise, Mr. Seselj? Then I will ask you whether you would like to raise anything and we close.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a feeling, Mr. Agius, that we are on different wavelengths. I never said that the detention unit was duty-bound to photocopy materials for me. But it is the Registry that is duty-bound to do so, in the same way that they provide administrative support to the Court and the Prosecution, they have to provide it to me. According to the Statute, I have the right to funds and means to prepare my defence, and one of the minimum requirements is the ability to photocopy. The response given to me is that the warden of the detention unit is not bound to do it. Well, he isn't, but the Court is. The Court has to provide me with means to prepare my defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I thank you. If you have an ad hoc motion to file in that regard, provided it is substantially different in argument from the previous one, you're free to do so and we will decide it. Yes, Mr. Saxon, are there any submissions you would like to make before we wind up?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have two very brief points to address the Court. First of all, simply that today the Prosecution intends to file a motion to admit a number of written statements pursuant to Rule 92 bis, so that will be filed by close of business today, Your Honour. Secondly, it is to the best of my understanding and belief, there is another matter still pending before the Chamber. It is the Prosecution's motion for non-disclosure of names and other identifying information which was filed on the 21st of July, 2004, and just very briefly, there is a bit of a history to this. It relates to a motion that the accused made in the end of March 2004 for access to all witness statements in the possession of the Prosecution that mentioned his name, and the Prosecution agreed to accept this motion as a request under Rule 66(B) with the caveat that certain witness statements that mention the accused's name also required certain redactions of identity, and so we filed a motion solely seeking permission from the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I recall it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And I believe that motion also is pending and, of course, that matter under Rule 66(B) could also move forward pursuant to the Trial Chamber's expected decision on form of disclosure once it's made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I reserve my position and that of the Trial Chamber on this. We'll check. I do, of course, have it -- I remember it vividly in my memory, but I am under the impression that we had come to a conclusion on that. I stand to be corrected and will deal with it after verifying. Any other submissions?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. So at this point, I declare the Status Conference closed. The next one will be held within the statutory or regulamentary period of 120 days and you will both be notified accordingly. Thank you.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the Status Conference adjourned at
